children: Gold and silver gave up earlier gains post-market Wednesday after the U.S. Federal Reserve
for the first time since 2023 and signaled that more tightening may be needed to contain inflation, sending the dollar higher and hurting non-yielding precious metals.
After-hours, gold for December delivery was trading near $4,302/oz, down 0.7%, and December silver slipped to $63.42/oz, down 0.6%, after rising sharply in regular trading.

The central bank raised the target range for the federal funds rate by 25 bps to 3.75%-4.0%, in line with consensus expectations, and the updated projections showed 16 of 18 Fed officials saw at least one more hike by year-end.
Fed Chairman Warsh said inflation remains too high, and the market read the decision as more than a one-and-done response to oil-driven price pressure.

"Our predominant focus is on the price stability side of our mandate. The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long. This summer's inflation readings do not tell ​me that ⁠underlying trends have meaningfully improved," Warsh said.

"Warsh's comments are being read as hawkish on top ​of a hawkish dot plot, which reinforces the view that there will be additional hikes ​in the upcoming meetings. That is helping the dollar and will pressure metals in the short-term," independent ‌metals ⁠trader Tai Wong told Reuters.
